articles.title: Guarding Stars review – Leighton Meester is a delight in fizzy Netflix holiday romance
articles.description: As a female bodyguard protecting an A-list star, the Gossip Girl actor shines in Christmas movie a cut above the competition Though it is my personal opinion that Christmas should not begin until after Thanksgiving, I am pleased to say that we already have at least one treat in Netflix’s holiday movie assembly line: Guarding Stars, starring Leighton Meester as a frosty bodyguard tasked with protecting Jared Padalecki’s movie star at, of all places, his family’s Montana ranch, falls on the fizzy side of seasonal fluff. Good holiday movies are an exercise in knowing silliness, and so it is a relief when the first 10 minutes of this movie, directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum, strikes the rare December balance between hearth-like warmth (the twinkle in Meester’s chocolate eyes when her Hannah Brooks lands a verbal punch) and complete lunacy (she lands that punch in an argument with her ex about … cuddling … literally seconds after thwarting an assassination attempt in Times Square). As a homespun band of hot would-be cowboys later drawl at a Christmas parade in “Montana” (Canada, per usual): “Christmas is back, y’all.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Anthropic sets share price at $83 for stock market debut, above expected range
articles.description: Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange. The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX. Continue reading...

articles.title: Shame is the only punishment in Australian cricket’s sandpaper scandal | Geoff Lemon
articles.description: The time for formal measures has passed but all involved have betrayed the trust of a country whose Test team is sacred Cry havoc. But Cameron Bancroft did not let anything slip, not after close to a decade of keeping his mouth firmly shut. It was a deliberate, considered and lengthy deed of revelation that the former Test opening bat chose to publish in the West Australian newspaper on Wednesday, claiming to finally fill in a wealth of detail around Australian cricket’s 2018 cheating scandal that so many others seem to have gone to such lengths to keep concealed. It was also a devastating repudiation of Pat Cummins, a teammate of equivalent juniority to Bancroft during their few months playing together, but now the Test captain, who had delivered his own manifesto in spoken form at a press conference last week. That version of events, in which Cummins was adamant that he had never been aware of any kind of ball-tampering in Australian colours, was what pushed Bancroft from silence to speech. “It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone,” Bancroft wrote. “What I saw, experienced and lived with not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
articles.description: A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies “Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement. The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
articles.description: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. articles.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
articles.description: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place ( BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November ). The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. articles.description: Not even a compelling TV drama can stop me from staring at my phone. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature I blame the shuffle button. That’s what started me on the long road to a thoroughly scattered mind – generally unable to focus on anything for more than a few minutes or even seconds. I was always a bit like this, hence an ADHD diagnosis in later life. But back in the day I still managed to read a lot of books, watch long films and listen to whole records at one sitting. Now? Not so much. Actually, hardly ever. Even something on television that I’m really engaged in – a drama or a football match – can hold me for only a few minutes before I find myself scrolling on my phone looking for I know not what. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. Where else can you indulge in a world of pure imagination, see the future – and chat over a curry with some of contemporary music’s biggest names? The Huddersfield contemporary music festival – or hcmf , with contemporary-cool lower-case, as it’s styled – celebrates its 49th edition this month, turning the darkness of late November into a beacon of blazing new-music ambition in West Yorkshire. It’s a festival with an extraordinary history. Nowhere else in the UK could you have bumped into Karlheinz Stockhausen and his entourage in a pub in the late 1980s; nowhere else could you have sat in the audience alongside Björk at the town hall; in no other town might you have stumbled on Pierre Boulez, John Cage, Olivier Messiaen and Yvonne Loriod chatting about the best place to have a curry that night. articles.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
articles.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green monochrome screen, but it also came with Tetris and worked for ages on four AA batteries. With sales of 65m, it was vastly more successful than hi-tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear. Continue reading...

articles.description: He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original ‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.” Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats. In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. articles.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
articles.description: National Gallery, London Bringing together all the pioneering master’s portraits for the first time reveals the way he clinically preserved monsters, merchants – even his wife – like flies in amber Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean? The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck. The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on with his brother Hubert. These too have portraits in them, of real people in uncanny proximity to supernatural beings. You could argue this show cheats by cutting out that medieval context of prayer and faith. It’s also a great way for the gallery to show off that it owns three of his greatest portraits. Yet the result makes you see the utterly strange way he collects his slightly miniaturised people like flies in amber. Continue reading...

articles.description: A 36-year fight for justice is explored in the galling HBO documentary When a Witness Recants. The three subjects and producer Coates explain how it unfolded For most of his life, the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates would occasionally think of a chilling episode from his childhood in West Baltimore: almost exactly 43 years ago, on 18 November 1983, a 14-year-old boy named DeWitt Duckett was shot and killed in a hallway of Harlem Park junior high school in the middle of the afternoon, by an older teenager who stole his blue satin Georgetown jacket. Coates was only eight at the time, too young to know the details, but old enough to perceive the collective horror around him. The sensational event – the first time a kid was killed inside a Baltimore public school, according to wall-to-wall local press – was a rupture in his child’s view of the world. “It was first time I had the sense that, oh, actually, I exist in a very dangerous world,” he told the Guardian. “And then you cut to the TV and it’s clear the rest of America is not existing in that dangerous world. The dangerous world is only for you and people who look like you.” Coates always assumed that the three teenage boys arrested and convicted for the murder were the right guys, and the episode faded into one of those strange imprints from the past, a blurry but foundational event. articles.description: Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style. Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “ gjak ” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Back in September, Turkish authorities began a large-scale crackdown on LGBTQ+ organizations and activists, raiding offices, blocking social media accounts and websites, arresting at least 116 people and launching criminal investigations into at least 160 people. Meanwhile, since last month, Turkey’s last two remaining opposition television channels have been brought under government control. This follows the Turkish government’s widespread crackdown on the main opposition party with dozens of mayors arrested since 2024. Despite Turkey’s authoritarianism, in Antalya, many of the Turkish groups critical of the government gathered in large numbers at the People’s Climate Summit, an alternative gathering to the U.N. climate summit organized by a coalition of Turkish environmental groups. For more, we hear from a number of activists from across Turkish civil society, including Berkan Özyer, the director of Greenpeace Türkiye, who tells us that “the more oppressive [a] regime gets, the more resilient people become.”

articles.description: As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms. The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today 4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxiety and depression, impeding their ability to work, they are often castigated as feckless snowflakes. It is easier to do this than admit that we have failed a generation, and that this is the predictable consequence of political decisions. articles.description: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. articles.title: A moment that changed me: the tomato pasta that became an obsession – and helped me lead a better life
articles.description: At a restaurant in Italy in 2022, every forkful of my meal made my eyes close and mouth water. For four years since, I have tried to recreate this dish. The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach. Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. I spent four days with his lovely family, in the rolling verdant hills, with fireflies and fallow deer keeping us company, drinking vernaccia and talking of books and art and poetry. But none of that matters, not even a bit. All that matters is a single plate of tomato pasta from Nuova Trattoria Albana , in Mazzolla, west of Siena. This pasta might have seemed, to the untrained palate, like any other pasta. But it changed everything for me. Continue reading...

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. More than 1.5 million people have already seen it in cinemas and its Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have picked up a roster of prestigious awards. Then, suddenly, there it was. A distant spout of water vapour. A humpback whale . As we motored out, more bushy plumes appeared to port and starboard, until we found the boat surrounded by about 15 individuals. Cutting the engine, the captain announced that he was about to employ a secret technique to coax the whales closer. There were raised eyebrows as the opening notes of Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On crackled over the speakers. articles.title: ‘The aesthetics in my family were so high, I felt ugly’: Charlotte Gainsbourg on extremism, abortion and her mother, Jane Birkin
articles.description: In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier While she was making the film Women on Trial , about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who helped her have an abortion, then illegal in France. The Bobigny trial was new to her, says Gainsbourg, who plays Halimi, a leading figure in French feminism and activism who died in 2020. “I had no idea. For me, abortion rights started with Simone Veil” – the French minister of health who saw through decriminalisation three years later – “so I had to catch up.” Continue reading...

articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. articles.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
articles.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. He may wear a lab coat and examine brain regions and neurochemicals, but studying the mechanics, he says, doesn’t damp down the mysteries of consciousness. “For me, actually, I’ve become more spiritual and interested in the world of mystery and, I want to say supernatural, but dimensions that are intangible, by studying something like sleep paralysis.” Continue reading...

articles.title: "Birds of War": New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon
articles.description: We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary Birds of War , which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the BBC , and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence. The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions. “Without our journalistic relationship, [we] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.” Birds of War premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.

articles.title: Meet David Morales: Providence Voters Elect Democratic Socialist Mayor, Approve Israel Divestment
articles.description: Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, approved a ballot measure last week that could result in the city divesting from Israel. The successful grassroots campaign makes Providence the first U.S. city to pass a binding divestment measure through a popular vote. The measure instructs the city to divest from countries and companies implicated in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The language does not mention Israel by name. We speak with one of the key backers of the divestment measure, Mayor-elect David Morales, a 28-year-old democratic socialist who made history on election night as the youngest mayor ever elected in Providence. “What we saw was our neighbors coming out in the thousands to demonstrate that we are ready for change,” Morales says, promising to enact his affordability-focused platform. “It’s the responsibility of local government to take action. And for that reason, we are seeing a rise in democratic socialism and the representation of democratic socialists all across the country.”

articles.title: "American Scoundrel": From Roy Cohn to Stephen Miller, "McCarthyism Lives On," Says Author Kai Bird
articles.description: We speak with historian Kai Bird about American Scoundrel , a new biography of the notorious political fixer Roy Cohn, who rose to fame as chief counsel to Joe McCarthy during the senator’s anti-communist campaign, served as a lawyer for the New York mob, and was an influential voice in Republican circles until his death from AIDS -related complications in 1986. His most impactful relationship, however, would prove to be with a young Donald Trump, whom he mentored in business and politics during the 1970s and ’80s. Facing political setbacks during his first term as president, Trump reportedly asked, “Where’s my Roy Cohn?” Bird, who co-authored American Scoundrel with his wife Susan Goldmark, says Trump may have found his Cohn in Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s mass deportation policies whom Trump just elevated to chief of staff. “It’s not really a surprise that, cornered and wounded by the recent election results, he reaches out and pulls up Stephen Miller, who’s very similar in his willingness to go on the offensive and never back down, and to say outrageous things to try to change the narrative,” says Bird.

articles.title: "The Earth Shook Last Night": Talarico Wins Senate, Hinojosa Becomes First Latina Governor in Texas
articles.description: Texas Democrats have shattered more than three decades of Republican dominance in the state, winning races for U.S. Senate, governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general and even railroad commissioner. They are also poised to possibly take control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2003. The Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, lost his bid for a fourth term to Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa, who defeated him by nearly 700,000 votes. She will be Texas’s first Latina governor. And James Talarico will be the first Democrat to represent Texas in the U.S. Senate since 1993. “We’re celebrating these wonderful candidates who won office, and we’re also starting to think about what it means to hold power,” says Mike Siegel, a city council member from Austin, Texas, who founded Ground Game Texas, a statewide voter turnout organization. “We need to start thinking very quickly about how we will protect public education, how we will stop data centers and the encroachment of AI on our society, how we will protect public schools, how we stop collaboration with ICE .”

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed Becomes First Muslim Senator as Democrats Rout GOP Across the U.S. in Rebuke to Trump
articles.description: In a stunning repudiation of President Trump, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. Meanwhile, progressive Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican Congressmember Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat in Michigan with over 52% of the vote. El-Sayed campaigned on a platform of Medicare for All, tackling economic inequality and getting big money out of politics — as well as ending military aid to Israel. He is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. El-Sayed faced vitriolic, Islamaphobic attacks by top Republicans throughout the campaign. “Last night wasn’t just about Dr. Abdulrahman being a Muslim, winning and going to the United States Senate,” says Palestinian American organizer and author Linda Sarsour, who has been campaigning for El-Sayed. “It demonstrated that progressives can win in states like Michigan” and that “we can win on standing up for the human rights of the Palestinian people.”

articles.title: The Last Spy review – a riveting tale of CIA meddling, espionage gossip and Blue Nun wine
articles.description: Refugee Peter Sichel was known as ‘the Jewish James Bond’ after fleeing Germany and becoming an integral cold war-era spy. He died last year but, at 100-years-old, he told his remarkable story for this film Why, exactly, was Peter Sichel “the last spy”? It’s not something Katharina Otto-Bernstein’s documentary about the cold war-era CIA man clarifies. The “Jewish James Bond” – as a woman from his synagogue nicknames him – is a catchier moniker, although that’s not quite right either. If Sichel was once a swashbuckling secret agent, we don’t hear much about his escapades here. Instead, he seems closer to M: sitting behind a desk pulling strings while his agents risked life and limb sneaking around the German Democratic Republic. The Last Spy begins as a straightforward but riveting biography built around a long, candid interview with Sichel, who was 100 at the time of filming (he died last year at 102). We hear about his childhood in Germany, which was initially privileged thanks to his great-grandfather’s lucrative wine business. Yet his mother was spooked early on by the rise of Hitler, and insisted the family relocate to France. When war did break out, all Germans were considered “enemy aliens” and sent to internment camps. Later, when the German army advanced, the Jews were allowed to make a run for it, pursued by warplanes. After hiding out near the Pyrenees, Sichel and his family escaped to New York in 1941 – only to find themselves living beside a Nazi-supporting neighbourhood on the Upper East side. Continue reading...

articles.title: Rassie Erasmus’s tired ref-blaming act is wearing thin – South Africa deserve better | Robert Kitson
articles.description: Springboks’ achievements are remarkable but their head coach lacks statesmanship, diplomacy and good grace in defeat So here we go again. Exactly five years have passed since South Africa’s head coach, Rassie Erasmus, first felt the full force of World Rugby’s ire for criticising match officials. And guess what? This most habitual of offenders has just copped another lengthy ban – and deservedly so – for his latest intemperate comments, notable as ever for their total lack of statesmanship, diplomacy or good grace in defeat. To his acolytes his outspoken nature is part of what makes Rassie such a groot leier (great leader). To many others it simply cements his status as a serial prat. For the avoidance of any doubt everyone respects the remarkable achievements both of Erasmus and his double World Cup-winning teams. It is the rest of the package, sadly, that is too often a major letdown. Continue reading...

articles.title: Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone
articles.description: He lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report? It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone. What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security . Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
articles.description: This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate. Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work , he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit. articles.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
articles.description: Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year. “The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis , ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation. articles.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
articles.description: The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over. Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. articles.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.description: With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south. Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions. Continue reading...

articles.title: Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep | Miatta Fahnbulleh
articles.description: I am at Cop31 – concerned about the crisis around the world, but mindful that voters want jobs, warmer homes and cheaper prices Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis. That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work. Continue reading...

Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed underpants off the clothesline just to make the long drive through the night worth it. articles.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
articles.description: Royal Academy, London The modernist collector once ran a gallery in London – but from this confusing exhibition, it’s hard to tell what exactly was once in there Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky , Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy . How to demonstrate the pioneering qualities of a gallery that is now a ghost? With reassembling and contextual padding, it appears. The catalogue states that at least 60% of the artworks in this exhibition were originally shown at Guggenheim Jeune, though only a handful of captions list definitive instances. Does this imply that where not stated, they are included for illustrative purposes? This may be due to relevant works being difficult to obtain; for the segment representing Jean Cocteau’s exhibition in January 1938 we have one of his ink drawings for his 1937 play Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde, and another in reproduction only. articles.title: A heretical outrage: why Italians disown spaghetti bolognese
articles.description: Spag bol carries my city’s name all over the world – to the embarrassment of restaurants in Bologna In Bologna, spaghetti bolognese does not exist. You’ll find it on menus in London and Sydney, in British school canteens and in jars on supermarket shelves across half the world, but not in the city that lent it its name. Order it in a trattoria beneath the Two Towers and at best you get a pitying smile. More often you’ll be brought a plate of tagliatelle, with a short lesson in local history on the side. Few of the Italian dishes famous abroad carry the name of a city. Every so often the argument flares up again over where pizza, carbonara or tiramisu were born. With spaghetti bolognese the parentage is written into the name, and yet, absurdly, it is the Bolognese themselves who disown it. Many regard it as an outrage, a heretical and misshapen version cooked only by people who know nothing of real Bolognese food. Continue reading...

The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that these physical media hold. Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic . “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.” Continue reading...

articles.title: I got scammed on Instagram – and it led to a truly disgusting dinner | Zoe Williams
articles.description: Intrigued by an unusual recipe for spinach tacos, I followed the instructions, but was left with a soggy, inedible mess. It turns out there are a lot of made-up meals out there I can’t tell you when my Instagram algorithm changed, from – this is embarrassing, but what the hell – buff guys trying to exercise and being interrupted by a Staffordshire bull terrier who wants to help them exercise, to cooking videos, but it has. I now get endless food content, following the same format: a millennial has 20 minutes to make dinner for his or her beloved (it’s very gender neutral), and launches into some unlikely techniques. He might shove a load of chicken into a cake tin, sprinkle mismatched spices all over, bake it, then slice it, as if it were a cake. Or she might cook tagliatelle in a pan of milk and salmon. This is not how it’s done, I think, as I watch all the way to the end, and then am astonished to be fed yet more weird food content. Drawn with an almost zombified lack of free will, I got the yen to try it for myself. What would happen if you boiled a white cabbage whole, then roasted it in honey and miso? Well, I can tell you: the cabbage is very soft on the outside, and still uncooked on the inside, and this is why cooks, since time began, have been slicing a cabbage before they try to cook it. A sliver of hope is the trio of doctors it profiles, individuals acting on their conscience. (The same can be said of director Poh Si Teng , who quit her job at ABC News and cashed in her savings to get the documentary off the ground.) It follows three American doctors who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital in southern Gaza in early 2025 – though one of the trio, Thaer Ahmad, an ER doctor of Palestinian heritage from Chicago, is refused entry the night before they enter Gaza. His colleagues, Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon, and Dr Mark Perlmutter, a Jewish-American orthopaedic surgeon, complete the mission. This is not the first time in Gaza for either of them. Before he leaves, Perlmutter packs antibiotics into a dozen or so little plastic bags dotted around his luggage; that way if he gets turned back at the border, he stands a chance of getting some of the life-saving medication through. Given the high death rate of medics in the war, he also gets a will drawn up before he goes. Continue reading...

articles.title: Rocky is Philadelphia’s founding myth – and 50 years later, we’re still telling it
articles.description: As Sylvester Stallone’s Oscar-winning drama celebrates its 50th anniversary, I Play Rocky helps to further turn the boxing hero into the stuff of legend The story behind the making of Rocky has always sounded uncannily like Rocky itself. An unknown with an improbable dream, a skeptical establishment and a refusal to accept the odds: Sylvester Stallone’s real-life struggle to crack the industry and bring his breakthrough film to the screen contained all the elements of the underdog story he sought to tell. Now, half a century later, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky has crafted those parallels into a crowd-pleasing yarn of its own. It’s an extraordinary afterlife for a modest boxing flick that became the highest-grossing film of 1976 on a $1m budget and won the Oscar for best picture over one of the most stacked fields in history. Yet its greatest achievement may be the durability of the story – dismissed then by the New York Times as a “sentimental little slum movie” and Gene Siskel as a “flatout schmaltzy saga” – that we’re still finding new ways to repurpose all these years later through six Rocky films, three Creed sequels, a Broadway musical , and too many documentaries, novelizations and video games to count. At some point long ago, a screenplay written in three and a half days and never envisioned as IP became something closer to contemporary folklore. Continue reading...

articles.title: The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking | Isobel Lewis
articles.description: The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele. The so-called sorry state of the vegan restaurant scene has been widely reported on (not least by me ). But after working with the food magazine Vittles on its inaugural London vegan guide , I have begun to challenge the “death of vegan dining” narrative that I had found myself perpetuating. And yes, a depressing number of my choices for the Vegan 99 closed while I was writing it; most recently, an omnivorous Malaysian restaurant with a walloping double-tofu laksa, which shut 24 hours before publication. But the process encouraged me to take a different viewpoint, instead focusing on the spots that had survived and the story they told. Isobel Lewis is a freelance culture and lifestyle journalist Continue reading...

articles.title: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. So what happens next?
articles.description: The wait for the new Bond is over but that’s only the beginning – there are still small issues such as the script, title, setting, casting, branding and promotion … • Robert Pattinson announced as James Bond – news • Share your thoughts on the casting • Peter Bradshaw’s take • Pattinson’s journey to James Bond • Behind Bond’s bankability It’s official: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond . While never a certainty for the role, for those reading the runes inside the film industry, the announcement will have been a tiny bit anticlimactic. Ever since it emerged that the film’s producers appeared unsatisfied with their initial shortlist and called in Pattinson alongside Nicholas Hoult, it appeared that in this new era for Bond under Amazon MGM, the traditional Bond barrier against an established Hollywood leading man was no longer in place. And with no shade to Hoult, Pattinson’s record at delivering in major franchises – Twilight, The Batman, Dune – as well as his classy acting CV put him firmly in the driving seat. In another departure from traditional 007 practice, Amazon MGM announced the casting decision via posts on social media , rather than at a press call in a fancy London hotel, which is how the world officially found out about George Lazenby, Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan . Although this will have been thought through as a way to maximise audience engagement with the forthcoming film, it perhaps is a disappointment to Bond purists that a big show wasn’t staged, and it may be Amazon MGM’s next order of business to organise a fan-type convention – or even piggyback on the next big fanclub event, due in December – to present Pattinson to an adoring audience. articles.title: Heysel 85 review – rage-filled denunciation of the incompetence that fuelled a football disaster
articles.description: Teodora Ana Mihai and her passionately committed cast reconstruct the grim sequence of bad judgments that led to 39 fans dying Shame and rage are the keynotes of this immersive, viscerally powerful drama-thriller set amid the macabre tragedy of football’s 1985 European Cup final between Juventus and Liverpool in the crumbling Heysel stadium in Brussels. Crowd disorder before kickoff in a poorly maintained, badly policed venue resulted in the deaths of 39 fans. In this film, the roar of the crowd echoing overhead through the stadium’s claustrophobic tunnels is like the wailing of the damned, while the sport’s officer class flinch and panic as if at a wartime loss. Grimly, the match was allowed to go ahead, despite the fatalities; the authorities believed the game itself would restore order on a bread-and-circuses basis, and that abandoning the match would only cause greater violence and chaos. Heysel 85 is directed and co-written by Romanian-born and Belgian-based film-maker Teodora Ana Mihai; she is a former collaborator of Cristian Mungiu, though maybe the influence here is more Paul Greengrass. The film-makers have been criticised for fictionalising aspects: the players are depicted as not being aware that fans had died before they took to the field – they were in fact largely aware, although it may well be true that the slippery authorities sought to minimise the truth as much as they could. And the fictionalised mayor of Brussels, here named Marc Dumont (Josse De Pauw), has been criticised as an unfair drunken caricature of the actual mayor, Hervé Brouhon. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Brightness by Chad Harbach review – an ambitious sequel to The Art of Fielding
articles.description: Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthood Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place. Legend has it that Harbach laboured over The Art of Fielding for more than a decade. When it finally emerged, a feverish bidding war saw it sell for more than $650,000 (£431,000), a saga chronicled at length in Vanity Fair. Any follow-up to such a high-profile debut, let alone one 15 years in the making, was always going to be read against the original. The Brightness, set on the same campus and peopled by many of the same characters, all but demands direct comparison. Throw in the fact that Harbach’s first novel actually turns up inside its sequel, and we’re in metatextual heaven. In the four years of Westish time that have elapsed between the two books, Owen Dunne (baseball player in The Art of Fielding; groom-to-be here) has written and published, to great acclaim, a novel called – guess what! – The Art of Fielding. articles.title: ‘His wife was horrified’: did Edward Hopper paint his sexual problems?
articles.description: He is the maestro of American melancholy. But in a new biography, the artist is called a ‘sadist’ and a ‘prize hog’ by his wife – who was aghast to see their domestic and bedroom problems surface in his most famous works It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.” Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. Jo once contemplated writing her husband’s biography herself, having amassed such an overwhelming body of material documenting their tumultuous marriage. As Edward’s creative partner, muse, curator, producer and unofficial manager, Jo produced 35 years’ worth of daily diaries, almost 100 notebooks, reels of letters, and four ledger books documenting Edward’s works. articles.description: It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing? In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate . In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble. Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m . Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious. Stamp was arrested for suspected breaches of the Financial Services and Markets Act: the FCA believed it had evidence he was offering financial services, such as debt and investment advice, without a licence. The day he was arrested, police also raided an industrial estate in Chessington, south-west London, where Stamp’s company had its offices, and seized dozens of computers and files. articles.title: Meet Will Lawrence: Sunrise Movement Co-Founder Elected to Congress on Anti-Data Center Platform
articles.description: Progressive candidate Will Lawrence of Michigan has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping the state’s 7th Congressional District, a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence, the co-founder of the youth-led climate organization Sunrise Movement, refused corporate PAC money, instead building a people-powered grassroots mobilization campaign. He focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, opposing the war on Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech. “I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development,” says Lawrence. “These developers come into small towns, and they say, ’We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.’” Lawrence also says he will back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, but that he will demand Democratic leadership listen to progressive concerns.

articles.title: "We Have to Be Brave": Palestinian Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh Speaks Out After Israeli Detention
articles.description: The prominent journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested on Wednesday by armed police and Shin Bet agents who conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. Abu Shehadeh’s detention was related to his reporting on the October 27 Israeli election and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the election, he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a Palestinian intellectual and former member of the Israeli Knesset who has lived in exile in Qatar since fleeing Israel amid allegations that he aided Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of “contacting a foreign agent,” in connection to his interview with Bishara. “Men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children,” says Shehadeh. “It tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.”

articles.title: Pentagon Whistleblower Wes Bryant: Impeach Hegseth. He's a "Clear & Present Danger" to Democracy
articles.description: The House of Representatives is moving toward a vote this week on whether to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday. They include violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran after Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop, illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing “extrajudicial killings” by bombing the boats of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, abducting President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for his participation in a video reminding troops not to obey illegal orders. If the House votes for impeachment, it will prompt a Senate trial that could end with removal from office. “Under Hegseth, the U.S. military has been hijacked,” says retired Air Force Master Sergeant Wes Bryant, who served as chief of civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon from 2024 to 2025. “America has portrayed itself to the world as a far-right dictatorship bent on global domination, and Hegseth and his wielding of the U.S. military with free rein from Donald Trump is really the primary enforcer of that.” Bryant adds that “Hegseth should be the first domino,” but that Trump, as well as “many of our senior military leaders,” should also be impeached.

articles.title: Latino Voters Swing Away from Trump for "Terrorizing Our Communities": Marisa Franco of Mijente
articles.description: In 2024, Donald Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Hispanic voters, suggesting that a major realignment in party preferences might be underway. But just two years later, it appears much of that support has eroded. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump. We get a bird’s-eye view of what to expect from the Latino vote from Marisa Franco, the co-founder and director of the advocacy organization Mijente. While ICE brutality will be at the front of voters’ minds, she says, Democrats cannot continue to take Latino voters for granted. “The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation,” explains Franco. “And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control. So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them.”

articles.title: Election Protection: NAACP on Voter Suppression & Deployment of Federal Poll Monitors
articles.description: As President Donald Trump continues to cast doubt on the integrity of U.S. elections, signaling his intentions to challenge results unfavorable to Republicans, we go to Washington, D.C., where a federal judge ruled Monday night that the Department of Justice can deploy election monitors to polling sites across the country, as long as they are not law enforcement officers with the power to make arrests. “In some respects, this is a victory for voters. Every voter in our country deserves to be able to cast a ballot today, free from intimidation,” says Kristen Clarke of the NAACP , which sued to challenge the DOJ’s plans to deploy ICE agents and other armed officers to the polls. The NAACP was also part of a coalition that intervened when the Trump administration attempted to force California to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that it alleged were sent incorrectly to noncitizens. “This was a baseless, error-prone, shoddy 11th-hour attempt to hijack the election in California, plain and simple, and it’s now been rejected by four courts,” Clarke says. The administration’s attacks on voters “are not bearing fruit,” she adds. “We anticipate and are ready for anything that they may throw our way.”

articles.description: Welcome to Mysterious Universe Season 36, episode 11! According to Buddhist doctrine, Agartha is a subterranean land located deep within the center of our planet. articles.title: Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction | Jonathan Horn
articles.description: Nothing about the responses and reprisals to Australia’s ball tampering have been proportional in a story where the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle Who said long-form journalism is dead? As Matt Renshaw nudged his ones and twos in an already forgotten ODI match, the broadcasters were scanning Cameron Bancroft’s 4000-word essay . SEN’s Gerard Whateley was calling for a comprehensive judicial inquiry, “a little bit like a coroner’s inquest,” with witnesses compelled to attend and be subjected to cross examination. Cricket Australia’s “forum” , announced a few hours earlier, had already been skittled. Nothing in the eight years since a piece of sandpaper was taken on to the field in Cape Town, including the publication of Usman Khawaja’s book Sabr , had been as revelatory as Bancroft’s first-person account . But as always with this story, we were bracing for the next press conference, the next podcast, the next corroborating statement, the next counterclaim, the next overreaction. Continue reading...

articles.title: Terror on Bondi Beach review – these astounding stories recreate every single second of horror
articles.description: From agonised parents trying to find their children, to the man who tackled a gunman – these gripping accounts of the 2025 Sydney attacks should never be forgotten Milo Riley-Smith’s documentary is a simple piece of diligent work. It begins by spending a short time gathering the backstories of its interviewees: how they or their parents came to Australia seeking a new life, finding it to be a welcoming place where, as one woman remembers, Jews “could have a fair go” because anyone could, whatever their ethnicity. These Jewish Australians then talk about how, after Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel and Israel’s subsequent bombardment of Gaza, they began to feel less safe. They had seen a flaring of antisemitic violence, vandalism and rhetoric; they attended the annual Hanukah festivities at Sydney’s Bondi beach with some trepidation. After an extended account of the events of 14 December 2025, the documentary’s participants comment briefly on whether enough was done by the Australian authorities to protect them. articles.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people. Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll . That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial
articles.description: A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another. This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives. articles.title: The Guardian view on Grand Theft Auto VI: a game that makes players think twice | Editorial
articles.description: For almost 30 years, Grand Theft Auto has revelled in America’s vices. Its latest instalment may find room for empathy amid the mayhem The biggest global cultural event of the year may not be something that millions of people watch together but somewhere that millions of people venture separately. In the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, players inhabit a fictionalised America through the eyes of two lovers turned cons in a rags-to-riches crime epic. On Thursday, when the game was released, workers called in sick and students skipped lectures to play at home. Such is GTA VI’s appeal that it is forecast to rake in billions of dollars within months. The game has been billed as a satire of American capitalism, and it is undoubtedly a landmark in interactive storytelling and art. The commercial success of its previous titles has rivalled that of Hollywood blockbusters. Playing GTA VI, as the Guardian’s video games editor observes , is like losing yourself in a doorstop novel, with hours of solitary immersion in a vividly conjured place – not a facsimile of modern Miami, but an interpretation, almost the size of Manchester , rendered with astonishing precision by the artists who designed, wrote, coded and soundtracked its virtual world. articles.title: Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI | Letter
articles.description: Berthold Schoene responds after the head of Ofqual said students could be disqualified from GCSEs and A-levels if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework Is this really the best we can do: draconically penalise the young for making use of the latest cognitive resources and tools available to them ( Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat, 18 November )? Our generation has allowed the introduction of “life-altering” new technologies into every walk of life without much democratic debate, public scrutiny or governmental oversight. And now our education leaders are threatening to jeopardise young people’s career prospects for deploying these technologies within an education system that can’t cope and struggles to adapt? We all know that AI is here to stay. And importantly, it is so much more than just a cheap cheating device. Within an incredibly short space of time, it has transformed how we work, communicate, solve problems, research and learn. Surely the pedagogical response cannot simply be to devise ever more elaborate ways of preventing students from using it? Continue reading...

articles.description: David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script, picking up from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and its lead is more ineffably beguiling than ever We got through to the very end of Quentin Tarantino’s previous film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood without finding out exactly how, why or if Brad Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth murdered his wife. It was an issue only addressed in Tarantino’s novel based on the movie. And throughout the 140 minutes of this outrageous sugar-rush sequel – scripted by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher – this subject is tactfully passed over in silence, the one point that damages our perception of Cliff’s amiable-cowpoke good nature. Cliff is the guy who climaxed the previous picture by helping with a dramatic rescue; after, that is, gallantly refusing an age-gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. Well, we may not get the complete picture of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover Cliff Booth novel, with which this film is to form a kind of multimedia narrative event. articles.description: Old-school Tory with a heart wants to make London fun again – just don’t mention Brexit Tories select James Cleverly as candidate for London mayor Sooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”. As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024 . A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate.
