articles.title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
articles.description: IMMA, Dublin From massacre locations painted on to basalt slabs to photocollages of bulldozed airports, artists from across the Levant address their traumatic history In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.” Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold. The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. The angry, melancholy, defiant work of these (mostly) Palestinian artists also weaves a traumatic national history into the cosmopolitan culture of the Levant and the interlinked world in which we now live. articles.description: It is the biggest game of the decade, but there are a billion reasons why GTA shouldn’t be adapted for television. It joins a list of wildly popular titles that won’t see the light of day on streaming platforms You probably aren’t going to see a Grand Theft Auto TV show anytime soon. Speaking on a recent podcast, Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of the game’s parent company Take-Two Interactive, said that a film or television adaptation of GTA would only happen if its team thought that it would “somehow engage and delight our consumers. It’s a high bar to do that. And, of course, there’s always a risk of failure. So we don’t rule it out, but we’re very, very selective.” And, well, good. There are a billion reasons why a small screen version would be a terrible idea. Creatively, the thrill of a GTA game is that no two players have the exact same experience. While you might spend your days mowing down civilians and bazookaing police helicopters out of the skies, someone else might take that time to go hiking or explore the waterways. articles.description: The cult film director and Moviedrome presenter answers your questions on why James Bond is anti-Russian propaganda, whether Christopher Nolan is a bore and wanting to save Hunter S Thompson Looking back, how do you regard your experience with Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas? And did you watch Terry Gilliam ’s version? AwapBamBoogers No, I didn’t watch it. I felt very sad about the whole thing because my wife and I were co-screenwriters. We went out to meet Hunter S Thompson and the poor guy was in a terrible state. He was hoovering up cocaine the whole time we were there. He had a great big TV screen, with a Post-it note saying: “Don’t watch too much TV.” We said we felt like his caseworkers, because all these guys in Hollywood like Johnny Depp were winding him up: “Dr Thompson, do something crazy, go out in the back garden and shoot a can of propane.” That’s all very well, but they were treating him like the freak in the county fairground. How many years was it after Fear and Loathing that the poor guy killed himself? He really needed an intervention. Instead, he was being encouraged by these Hollywood bastards. The giant boar in Razorback gave me nightmares when I saw it on Moviedrome . Did it give you nightmares too? Sootsayer I don’t remember. The films in Moviedrome were picked by [producer and director] Nick Freand Jones, who had access to all the films the BBC had under licence and didn’t know what to do with. articles.title: Abandoning a Cat by Haruki Murakami review – an intimate meditation on family and memory
articles.description: The author explores the life and legacy of his estranged father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world war When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.” Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime. articles.title: Flottiana album review – 10-cd collection celebrates a very, very great Dame
articles.description: Lott/Johnson (Hyperion) We lost a truly singular talent with the death of Dame Felicity Lott earlier this year. This box-set brings together some of the British soprano’s finest recordings When Dame Felicity Lott died in May this year, the world lost a truly singular talent. An effortlessly elegant soprano, Flott, as she was known, was as at home in German, and especially French, as she was in her native English. This 10-CD boxset from Hyperion brings together some of her finest recordings from a career that spanned half a century. It’s curated by Graham Johnson, who in 1976 recruited Lott for The Songmakers’ Almanac, the pioneering vocal ensemble whose mission was to explore neglected corners of the repertoire. First, the voice; an instrument that appears incapable of anything indecorous. It never spreads or strays from the note, maintaining a purity and brilliance even when hovering in the musical stratosphere. Then there’s the diction, crisp and clear, wedded to an intelligence that lays bare the inner meaning of a song without mannerisms or affectation. With Lott it was straight and to the point, every emotion subtly and honestly conveyed. Continue reading...

articles.title: How beaujolais conquered the snobs
articles.description: Beaujolais is enjoying something of a renaissance, with even much-maligned nouveau gaining ground thanks to the fashion for light, chilled, low-tannin reds “Oh, it’s beaujolais. Fantastic!” My earliest memory of beaujolais isn’t of drinking it, but of saying it, on stage, as Beverley in a school production of Mike Leigh’s Abigail’s Party . Leigh wrote the play a few years into the British craze for beaujolais nouveau, the just-made, casual quaffing wine – historically destined for local consumption in France – that’s released on the third Thursday of every November. Sold cheaply, it landed beaujolais with an image that belied its extraordinary variety and quality. It was, says The Encyclopedia of Wine , “a self-administered cataclysm” on beaujolais’ part. Nowadays, it’s common knowledge that there is more to beaujolais than beaujolais nouveau, from its most famous village crus, such as Fleurie, Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent, to higher-altitude, lesser-known villages that, amid the climate crisis, are now coming into their own. Beaujolais lies just south of Burgundy, in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, with mostly granite-based soils to the north (perfectly suited to the red gamay grape for which it is famous), and calcareous soils to the south (used to make its more elusive and underappreciated white wines, mostly from chardonnay). articles.title: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child
articles.description: Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “ no way” . Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty. Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple , Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Thanksgiving food traditions we could all share
articles.description: Warming pie, buttery mash and plenty of gravy are a perfect excuse to gather friends around the table during chilly November • Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast As a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. And yet, every November, as the days grow shorter and darker and colder, I find myself rather taken with the idea of hosting a seasonal dinner for friends. If Christmas is more formal and family-focused, then Thanksgiving feels like a prime opportunity to get pals around the table, eat until you need to undo your top trouser button, and take a moment to appreciate what you have. And if that means borrowing a few ideas from across the Atlantic – a warming spiced pumpkin pie , say, or a dish of fruity stuffing and a sharp cranberry sauce – well, there’s no reason we can’t make them our own. Obviously there are some crossovers with Britain’s main festive meal, turkey being the big one. Personally, I prefer to cook a cockerel on Christmas Day, which naturally gives me the opportunity to make turkey for Thanksgiving instead. Brining the bird in advance really is a gamechanger, and Margot Henderson’s buttermilk and harissa brine gives you the most succulent and aromatic meat. Rather than roasted, the potatoes are usually mashed and buttery, and if you are going to make that, then Joël Robuchon’s best mashed potatoes in the world are probably the way to go. Just remember, now is not the time to shy away from butter. articles.title: Is Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages the year’s wildest electronic album?
articles.description: (Warp) The Milan producer revisits his youth as a straight-edge punk fan voyeuristically dabbling in rave – and finds a thrilling interzone between both genres The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”. A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the icy, staccato notes and arpeggiated synth lines of the genre’s epic breakdowns into lengthy, beatless tracks that never reached the climax implied. Released at the height of the 2020 Covid lockdown – when everyone was, by default, some distance from the dancefloor – his last album, Scacco Matto , expanded his palette to include lush ambient electronics, quasi-classical chord structures and something of the teeming chaos of Rustie’s digital maximalism. articles.title: Robert Pattinson to apply for 90,000 more jobs? UK government trolls James Bond actor
articles.description: Westminster joins wave of ‘job-stealing’ memes after the actor’s late success edging out the other contenders to be the new 007 Everybody is trying to get a piece of the Bond action: even the UK government. In a post on its official Instagram account , the UK government promoted its youth jobs guarantee scheme, first announced in August , with a picture of Robert Pattinson as Bond with the joke caption: “Robert Pattinson to apply for all 90,000 jobs created for young people through Youth Employment Scheme.” Continue reading...
